reason: This book is a quality-momentum/trend-following mandate, and the single question a trend book must answer each week is whether the trend it is riding was confirmed or broken. It was confirmed, emphatically, by the event that sits between my 09-16 fill and today. The Fed raised rates 25bp on 2026-09-16 -- its first hike since 2023 -- the 10-year yield pushed above 5% for the first time since 2023, TLT touched $80 on Monday for its lowest print since July 2025 against a 52-week range of $80.46-$92.19, crude stayed elevated, European natural gas prices are surging, and XLE has now returned roughly 47% over a year after topping the August sector table at +7.4%. Every one of those is the thesis of this book restated by the tape. Trading here would mean replacing positions whose reason for existing was just externally validated, which is the classic way a trend follower converts a working signal into transaction costs. The leg itself is three sessions old and net positive: VLO +2.48%, GDX +2.89%, XLE +0.44%, with XOP -0.62%, DBC -0.69%, XME -0.08%, XLF -0.13% and the TLT short -0.46% all inside two days of noise and none of them anywhere near their stops. There is no signal in that dispersion to act on; a 0.46% adverse mark on a short into a week when the Fed hiked is a pause in a trend, not a reversal, and TLT at the bottom of its 52-week range with a 5%-plus long end and freshly hawkish policy is exactly where a duration short should be held rather than covered. The one leg I genuinely examined for removal was XLF at 8%, since a hiking Fed can flatten or invert the curve and financials are owned here for steepening; I keep it because the hike came with a long end that rose faster than the front, which steepens rather than flattens, and because 8% is small enough that being early costs little. Against all of this, replacing the book would cost real basis points -- roughly 2bps per side across 80% gross plus SEC/TAF on the sells -- to buy back substantially the same exposure, and it would reset every stop-loss to a worse level, since my current stops sit under entry fills struck before this week's confirming move. Holding also preserves the sharp separation from my Round 2 value book, which carries no ETF or commodity exposure and no short at all, so same-direction gross-weight overlap between the two remains far below the 50% limit on any reading, symbol-level or economic. The book is aligned with the macro, hedged by hard stops under every leg and a 20% cash position earning 4%, and the correct action for a trend follower whose trend is intact is to leave it alone and let the winners run.
